M365 Setup & File Organization Guide
Everything you need to create, name, save, and submit your work in this course. Keep this page open the first time you turn something in.
💻 1. HOW TO SIGN IN
Go to office.com and sign in with your Optima school account (the email Optima gave you, ending in your school domain). Do not use a personal Microsoft account. Your school account is the only one connected to this course and to OneDrive.
From the office.com home page you can open Word, OneDrive, and the rest of your apps in the browser. No download is required.
📁 2. YOUR ONEDRIVE FOLDER FOR THIS COURSE
Keep all of your work for this course in one place. In OneDrive, create this folder path if it does not already exist:
Optima → Electives → CRDM
To build it: open OneDrive, click New → Folder, name it Optima, open it, add a folder named Electives, open that, and add a folder named CRDM. Save every file for this course inside the CRDM folder so it is easy to find later.
📝 3. THE FILE NAMING RULE
Name every file the same way so your teacher and your future self can find it:
LastName_FirstName_AssignmentShortName_CRDM
Filled-in example:
Smith_Jane_IndustryTracker_CRDM
If an assignment asks for more than one draft, add _Draft1, _Draft2, and then _Final on the version you submit. Keep each draft as its own file; do not overwrite an earlier one.
📤 4. HOW TO SUBMIT THROUGH CANVAS
1
Open the assignment in Canvas and click Start Assignment (or Submit Assignment).
2
Choose the OneDrive tab. Sign in with your school account if Canvas asks.
3
Find your file in the Optima → Electives → CRDM folder, select it, and attach it.
4
Click Submit. Check that the file name shows on the confirmation. A PDF export is also accepted when an assignment allows it.
💡 5. I JOINED MID-YEAR. WHAT DO I DO?
Welcome. You can get set up on your own. Work through these in order:
☐
Confirm you can sign in at office.com with your school account. If you do not have one yet, message your teacher.
☐
Build your Optima → Electives → CRDM folder in OneDrive using Section 2 above.
☐
Review the file naming rule in Section 3, then bookmark this page so you can return to it.
☐
Message your teacher to ask whether any earlier assignments need to be made up, and which ones.
⚡ 6. WHERE TO GET HELP
Course questions: send your teacher a message in Canvas. Describe what you tried and where you got stuck so they can answer quickly.
How-to questions about Word and OneDrive: Microsoft keeps free beginner tutorials at support.microsoft.com. Search the app name and what you want to do, for example “OneDrive create a folder” or “Word save a copy.”

Warm-Up
Tool Tour: A Scavenger Hunt
Assignment · 15 pts · graded on completion
📋 ASSIGNMENT OVERVIEW
The Career Research Toolkit page lists the websites you will use all course. The fastest way to make them feel familiar is to actually open them once and find something. This short scavenger hunt does exactly that. There are no trick questions; you just need to visit the sites and report what you find. Open the Career Research Toolkit page in a second tab to get the links.
📝 FIND AND RECORD (answer each in a sentence)
1
BLS Occupational Outlook Handbook. Look up any one job that interests you. Write the typical entry-level education it lists and whether the field is projected to grow, shrink, or stay about the same.
2
O*NET My Next Move. Browse careers by interest, or run the Interest Profiler. Name one career it suggested that you had not considered before.
3
CareerOneStop / GetMyFuture. Use a finder to search your own area (your state or ZIP). Name one local training program, school, or apprenticeship it returned.
4
Your pick. Open one more site from the Toolkit (College Scorecard, studentaid.gov, apprenticeship.gov, CFPB, or the VA GI Bill page) and write one useful thing you found there and why it might matter to you.
💡 TRY THE OTHER TWO RESEARCH MODES TOO
For a bonus, pick one of your four answers and do two things: ask your school AI account to explain or expand on it (then check what it says against the site), and think of one person you could ask about it in real life. You will use all three research modes throughout the course.
✅ SUCCESS CRITERIA
☐
All four items answered, each based on something you actually found on the site.
☐
At least one answer names something specific to your own interests or your own area.
📤 SUBMISSION INSTRUCTIONS
Canvas Assignment Name: Tool Tour
Type your four answers directly in the Canvas text box and submit. This is graded on completion, so just be honest and specific.

Industry & Experts Setup
Assignment · 20 pts
📖 RESEARCH FOCUS
One industry, three vetted sources
Builds on Lesson 1.3
What you are creating: the starting page of your semester-long Industry Tracker, a short document naming the field you will follow and the credible sources you will follow it through.
📋 ASSIGNMENT OVERVIEW
Choose one industry to track for the semester. Then build a follow-list of three sources: one neutral anchor and two commentators you have personally vetted with the SIFT moves and the five questions from the lesson. For each source, write a few sentences on how it passed your check. This document is yours to keep adding to all semester, so set it up to last. If you already know someone who works in this field, jot their name at the bottom too: people are a source, and you will learn to reach out to them later in the course.
🎯 FOCUS QUESTION
Who is worth listening to about this field, and how do I know?
📁 M365 REMINDER
Create this in Microsoft Word from your school account. Name the file LastName_FirstName_IndustryTracker_CRDM and save it to your Optima → Electives → CRDM folder in OneDrive. Submit through Canvas using the OneDrive tab. Keep this file: you will add to it all semester.
M365 Skill You're Practicing: creating and naming a Word document; applying Heading styles.
📝 STUDENT DIRECTIONS
1
Name your industry. In one short paragraph, say which industry you will track and why it interests you. It does not have to be your future career.
2
Add one anchor source. Choose a neutral, fact-reporting source (for example the BLS Occupational Outlook Handbook or Pew Research Center). Give its name and link, and one sentence on what it will tell you about your field.
3
Vet and add two commentators. Find two writers, trade publications, or professionals who cover your field. For each, do a lateral read and write three to four sentences on how it did against the five questions (sources cited? multiple sources? corrections? transparent funding? goal to inform?).
4
Flag one you rejected. Name one source you considered but decided not to trust, and explain the red flag in a sentence or two. Vetting includes saying no.
✅ SUCCESS CRITERIA
☐
An industry is named with a clear, honest reason for choosing it.
☐
One neutral anchor source and two vetted commentators are listed with working links.
☐
Each commentator has a real vetting note that uses the SIFT moves or the five questions, not just “seems legit.”
☐
One rejected source is named with its red flag.
📊 GRADING RUBRIC
Criteria Proficient Developing Pts
Industry choice & rationale
5 pts		 A clear industry and a specific, honest reason for choosing it. Industry named but the reason is vague or missing. 5 pts
Quality of source vetting
9 pts		 Vetting notes apply the SIFT moves or five questions with real reasoning for each commentator. Notes are present but thin, generic, or do not show a lateral read. 9 pts
Complete, usable follow-list
6 pts		 Anchor, two commentators, and one rejected source, all with working links and named per the file rule. Missing a source, a link, or the rejected example; or file not named correctly. 6 pts
Total: 20 pts
📤 SUBMISSION INSTRUCTIONS
Canvas Assignment Name: Industry & Experts Setup
Submit your Word document (.docx) through Canvas using the OneDrive tab. A PDF export is also accepted.
Keep this file. You will return to it throughout the course as your field changes.

Assignment · 10 pts · graded on completion
📋 ASSIGNMENT OVERVIEW
Lesson 2.2 gave you two tools: the Eisenhower Matrix for sorting tasks, and SMART for turning a wish into a goal you can steer by. This assignment has you use both on your own real week, not a hypothetical one. You will sort your actual current tasks, write one real SMART goal tied to a path or plan you are considering, break it into milestones, and put the first milestone on your actual calendar.
📁 M365 REMINDER
Create this in Microsoft Word from your school account. Name the file LastName_FirstName_PlanGoalBuild_CRDM and save it to your Optima → Electives → CRDM folder in OneDrive. Submit through Canvas using the OneDrive tab.
📝 STUDENT DIRECTIONS
1
Build your Eisenhower Matrix. List at least six real tasks currently on your plate, from any part of your life, and sort each one into the correct quadrant (Do Now, Schedule, Delegate or Trim, Drop).
2
Write one SMART goal. Using the five-row template from the lesson, write a goal tied to a path or plan you are actually considering. Fill in all five parts: Specific, Measurable, Achievable, Relevant, Time-bound.
3
Break it into milestones. List at least three milestones between now and the goal's deadline, each one small enough to act on.
4
Block the coming week. Pick your first milestone and write the specific day and time this week you will work on it. Use your phone calendar, Outlook, Microsoft To Do, or a VR whiteboard if you use one, and write down what you set.
✅ SUCCESS CRITERIA
☐
At least six real tasks are listed and sorted into the correct Eisenhower Matrix quadrant.
☐
One SMART goal is written with all five parts filled in and tied to a real path or plan.
☐
The goal is broken into at least three concrete milestones.
☐
The first milestone is blocked onto a specific day and time in the coming week.
📤 SUBMISSION INSTRUCTIONS

Module 2 Project
AI-Assisted Planning: Your First Draft
Assignment · 25 pts
📋 ASSIGNMENT OVERVIEW
You will use your school AI account as a research and drafting partner to build the first version of a 1-year and 5-year plan for yourself. This is a draft on purpose. You will revise it later in the course as you learn more, so the goal now is a real, honest starting plan, not a perfect one. The skill being graded is not "using AI." It is directing the tool well: asking sharp questions, checking what it tells you, and keeping the decisions and the words your own.
🎯 FOCUS QUESTION
Where do I want to be in one year and in five years, and what are the concrete steps to get there?
⚠️ USING AI WISELY AND SAFELY
Three rules for this assignment. First, verify facts: AI can state outdated or invented numbers and links with full confidence, so check any pay, cost, or program detail against a primary source from your Career Research Toolkit and cite it. Second, keep your own voice: the plan must read like you wrote it, because you did. Do not paste the AI's words as your final answer. Third, protect your privacy: do not share personal details you would not want stored. The judgment in this plan has to be yours; AI just helps you get there faster.
📝 STUDENT DIRECTIONS
1
Start from your own priorities. Open the Personal Stock Inventory you wrote in Lesson 1.4. Your plan must be built on your real strengths, interests, values, and the priorities you ranked, not on whatever the AI suggests first.
2
Research three ways. Use all three research modes from your Career Research Toolkit, not just one. Look facts up on trusted sites; ask the AI good questions to explore options and steps; and, if you can, ask a person who works in or near the field one real question. Strong AI prompts are specific, for example: "I am interested in [field] and I value [X]. What are realistic entry points after high school, and what would a sensible first year look like?" Save the three or four questions you found most useful; you will turn them in.
3
Draft the plan in your own words. Write a 1-year plan (concrete steps for the next twelve months) and a 5-year plan (the path those steps point toward). For each, include at least one specific action, one skill or credential to build, and one person or place to connect with (the networking habit).
4
Fact-check two claims. Pick two facts the AI gave you (a salary range, a program length, a requirement) and verify each against a primary source. Note what you checked and whether it held up.
5
Reflect briefly. In three or four sentences, say where the AI helped, where it was wrong or unhelpful, and what in the plan is a decision only you could make.
📝 WHERE TO DRAFT AND MAP YOUR PLAN
Plan wherever you think best. Many students sketch a 1-year and 5-year plan as a map or timeline before writing it up: do that in your notebook, on paper, or in a VR workspace where you can lay out steps on a whiteboard and rearrange them. VR is optional, never required. Your final plan is submitted as the Word document described below regardless of where you sketched it.
📁 M365 REMINDER
Write your plan in Microsoft Word from your school account. Name the file LastName_FirstName_CareerPlan_CRDM_Draft1 and save it to your Optima → Electives → CRDM folder. Keep this draft; you will revise it later as _Draft2. Submit through Canvas using the OneDrive tab.
✅ SUCCESS CRITERIA
☐
The plan is built on your own ranked priorities from Lesson 1.4, in your own words.
☐
A 1-year and a 5-year plan, each with an action, a skill or credential, and a connection to make.
☐
Two AI-provided facts are verified against named primary sources.
☐
A short reflection names where AI helped, where it failed, and what only you could decide.
📊 GRADING RUBRIC
Criteria Proficient Developing Pts
Plan grounded in your priorities
9 pts		 1-year and 5-year plans are specific, in the student's voice, and clearly built on their Lesson 1.4 priorities. Generic or AI-voiced; weak link to the student's own priorities. 9 pts
Wise, verified use of AI
10 pts		 Useful research questions saved; two facts verified against named primary sources with results noted. Little evidence of checking the AI; facts unverified or sources unnamed. 10 pts
Reflection on judgment
6 pts		 Names where AI helped, where it failed, and what only the student could decide. Vague or missing reflection. 6 pts
Total: 25 pts

📋 ASSIGNMENT OVERVIEW
You have now looked at the major paths after high school as peers: four-year and two-year college, trade and technical school, apprenticeships and other earn-while-you-learn on-ramps, military service, and going straight to work. In this assessment you put that to work on the only case that matters: yours. Choose two or three paths that genuinely interest you, research each one with real tools, compare them honestly for your situation, and make a tentative choice you can defend. The goal is not to lock in your future. It is to show that you can reason your way to a decision with evidence.
🎯 FOCUS QUESTION
Given what I want and what is true about these paths, which one fits me best right now, and why?
📝 STUDENT DIRECTIONS
1
Pick two or three paths. Choose the ones that actually fit your interests, values, and priorities from Lesson 1.4. Say in a sentence why each made your shortlist.
2
Research each one with real tools. For each path, pull current information from primary sources using your Career Research Toolkit (the reference page in Module 1): pay and outlook from the BLS Handbook or O*NET, cost and earnings by field from College Scorecard, and training and funding from CareerOneStop, Federal Student Aid, or apprenticeship.gov, all listed there. Where you can, also ask a person on the path what the data leaves out. Cite where each figure came from.
3
Compare them on the same questions. Use the five questions from Lesson 1.2 (cost and debt, time to earning, hands-on or academic, structure or independence, certainty or exploration), plus what you learned about funding and location in this module. A table is a good way to lay this out.
4
Make a tentative choice and defend it. Say which path fits you best right now and give the reasoning. A strong answer explains not just why you chose it but why you set the others aside.
5
Name what you still do not know. End with the honest open questions: what you would need to learn, try, or confirm before committing for real. This is part of the grade, not an afterthought.
📝 WHERE TO DO THIS WORK
Many students map a comparison like this before writing it up. Do that wherever helps: in your Word notebook, on paper, or in a VR workspace where you lay the paths out on a whiteboard and move the factors around. VR is optional, never required. Lesson 5.6 closed with the idea that getting the offer is a start line, not a finish line, and that the same habits that got you in the door, observing, asking good questions, and building a reputation on purpose, carry you through the first weeks. Write a short reflection that looks back at what you learned across this course and forward to your own first day.

📋 ASSIGNMENT OVERVIEW
Back in Module 2 you wrote a first draft of a 1-year and 5-year plan. Since then you have compared paths, learned to fund them, built a resume, and practiced applying and interviewing. Now you revise that draft into a real plan you can act on. This is the capstone of the course: proof that you can turn research and self-knowledge into a strategy. It is your plan, so it should reflect your honest goals, not a guess at what a teacher wants.
🎯 FOCUS QUESTION
What is my next year actually going to look like, and what is it building toward?
📝 STUDENT DIRECTIONS
1
Reopen your Module 2 draft. Save a new version named LastName_FirstName_CareerPlan_CRDM_Final so you keep the draft. Reread it with everything you now know.
2
Update the plan with what you learned. Name the path or two you are now aiming at, a realistic way to fund it, and the role your resume, network, and interview skills play. Look up any current figures using your Career Research Toolkit rather than guessing.
3
Make the 1-year plan concrete. List specific next steps for the coming year: applications, a credential or skill to build, people to contact, money to save or seek. Each step should be something you could actually start.
4
Sketch the 5-year direction. Where do the next-year steps point? You do not need certainty; you need a direction and a sense of what would move you along it.
5
Close with what changed. In a short paragraph, explain how your plan changed from the Module 2 draft and what in the course changed it. Name the open questions you still have.
📝 WHERE TO DO THIS WORK
Map the plan before you write it up if that helps: lay the next-year steps out as a timeline in your notebook, on paper, or on a VR whiteboard where you can reorder them. You may use your school AI account to research and to pressure-test the plan, but verify any figure and keep the words and decisions your own. The submitted plan is the Word document below.
📁 M365 SKILL
Revise in Microsoft Word using File → Save As to make the _Final version (keep your _Draft1). Save to your Optima → Electives → CRDM folder and submit through Canvas using the OneDrive tab.
M365 Skill You're Practicing: using version naming to keep a draft and a final (OneDrive / Word).

☐
A named path, a realistic funding approach, and concrete one-year steps.
☐
A five-year direction the one-year steps point toward.
☐
A closing paragraph on what changed since the Module 2 draft and the open questions that remain.
☐
Saved as a _Final version with the Module 2 draft kept.

12 pts		 Named path, realistic funding, and specific one-year steps that could actually be started. Vague path or steps; little funding thought. 12

9 pts		 The near-term steps clearly point toward the longer-term direction. Weak link between the one-year and five-year parts. 9

discussions.title: Discussion: One Honest Claim About Your Industry's Future
discussions.html:
Using a vetted source from your Industry Tracker (not a headline, not a hunch), state ONE specific claim about how your chosen industry is changing or will change, and explain WHY you believe it: what evidence or reasoning supports it? Name your source and link it. Keep your claim narrow and specific ("AI tools are taking over first-draft work for X, so workers there spend more time on Y") rather than broad ("AI will change everything"). > > Then reply to one classmate in a different industry. Do not just agree. Either strengthen their reasoning with another piece of evidence, or respectfully explain where you think it is too strong or too vague, and why. Use the "exposure is not the same as job loss" idea from Lesson 2.1 if it applies.

Rubric (15 pts):

  • Specific, sourced claim (7): a narrow claim, a named and linked vetted source, and real reasoning. (Thin/unsourced = partial; missing = 0.)
  • Substantive reply (5): strengthens or respectfully challenges a classmate with reasoning, not just agreement.
  • Uses module ideas (3): draws on task-vs-job, augmentation, or source-vetting from this module.
